Red, Granny Smith, Golden Delicious, Cox's Orange Pippin, Russet; Crab, Bramley, Arkansas Black, Pink Pearl. Just for looks: every kind bears ordinary apples.

Meat bird Black and green-sheened, the biggest chicken of them all. Eggs: some, brown. Size: many.

Dual-purpose Deep red-brown and tough. A good layer and a good table bird. Eggs: many, brown. Size: some.
Dual-purpose White with a black-flecked collar and tail: an old English all-rounder. Eggs: many, cream. Size: some.
Dual-purpose Barred black and white all over. Hardy, calm and productive. Eggs: many, brown. Size: some.
Dual-purpose Glossy black with a green sheen: the best layer of the all-rounders. Eggs: many, brown. Size: some.
A good egg and a good roast. The easiest first flock for a new farm.
One rooster is enough for a run of hens. Mixed breeds cross happily, and chicks may favour either parent. Keep the rooster with the hens: a Silkie needs one near to hatch chicks.

Kept for looks, and their gifts. Small, but a Silkie hatches her own chicks.

The brown barred farm quail of meadows and fields. The best layer: an egg every couple of minutes.
Chestnut, with a white throat and eye stripe. The wild quail of plains and field edges.
Blue-grey with a black face and a curling plume. Lives in savanna and scrub.
The tiniest quail, slate-blue and chestnut. Hides in jungle and warm grassland.

Quails live in small coveys. They eat seeds like chickens, breed with seeds, and lay speckled quail eggs. They are flighty: walk up openly and they scurry off. Sneak, or hold seeds, to get close. A fall never hurts them:
Quail eggs bake like any egg and fit a carton; thrown, one may hatch. Their barred feathers fletch arrows. Cook raw quail in a furnace, smoker or on a campfire.
They live between the bank and the water, floating at the waterline and dabbling. A drake and a duck, or a gander and a goose, pair up on seeds.
Ducks lay all year, Runners and Campbells most. Geese lay big eggs, in spring only; the Chinese most. A thrown duck or goose egg may hatch. Both birds give feathers, and roast well.
Table bird, lays well The big white farm duck: quick to grow for the table, and a good layer too.
Best layer Stands bolt upright like a bottle and runs rather than waddles. The best layer of all.
Prolific layer A plain khaki duck and a bronze-headed drake: a prolific layer.
Table bird Mallard colours on a heavy body. A slow layer, but a fine bird for the table.
Table bird, quiet Big and quiet, with red caruncles about the face; the drake wears a little crest.

Ornamental A white duck with a pom-pom crest, kept for the fun of it.
Walk up openly and a goose hisses, neck low; linger and a gander charges and nips. Creep up crouching, or carry seeds, to pass. A monster near the flock sets them honking.
Table bird The tall white goose of the farmyard: heavy, quick to grow, a fine table bird.
Table bird Grey, broad and heavy, with a deep keel and a dewlap under the bill.
Watch goose, best layer Slim and upright with a knob on its bill: a loud watch goose and the best layer. Grey-brown or white.
Ganders white, geese grey Auto-sexing: the ganders are white and the geese grey, so you can tell them at a glance.
Twelve breeds of sheep, for mutton, wool, milk or the heat; rams and ewes, shearing, and the black sheep; eight breeds of goat; and the Border Collie that fetches them in.
Meat · Quick-finishing lambs Black face and legs, a big frame. The classic meat ram; its lambs grow up quickly. Horns: none. Lands: temperate.
Meat · Heavily muscled Short, stocky and heavily muscled, with a clean white face. An extra cut of mutton. Horns: none. Lands: temperate.

Meat · Easy lambing A long, lean French sheep with a pinkish face. Ewes lamb easily, often twins. Horns: none. Lands: temperate.

Big, quick-growing sheep for mutton. Fatten them at a trough; a Texel gives an extra cut.
Wool · Fine fleece The finest wool there is, and lots of it. Rams carry big curled horns. Horns: rams. Lands: temperate.
Wool · Longwool Long lustrous locks to the ground: the heaviest fleece of any breed. Horns: none. Lands: temperate.
Wool · Twins and triplets A grey Russian sheep born black. Ewes have twins and triplets. Horns: none. Lands: cold, mountains.
Wool · Gentle Black face, black knees, curly fleece. Mountain sheep, horned both, and very gentle. Horns: rams and ewes. Lands: cold, mountains.
Wool comes in a sheep's own colour: cream, the Romanov's grey, or black. Dye a sheep and its fleece takes the dye. A lamb is born in its own wool, never its parents' dye.
Bred for heavy fleeces. Keep a Merino flock for the biggest clips.

Hair sheep · Sheds its coat A red-brown hair sheep from Brazil: long-legged, tough, and at home in the heat. Horns: none. Lands: hot.

Hair sheep for the heat, and a milking breed. Milk an East Friesian ewe with a bucket.

Heavy milker The big white Swiss dairy goat: calm, tall, and the heaviest milker of them all. Found in temperate meadows and plains.
Rich milk Long lop ears and a Roman nose; loud, and rich in milk. Tan or spotted. Found in hot country: the savanna.
Hardy A sturdy goat from the Alps, tougher than most and at home in the cold. Found up in the cold mountains and hills.

Rich milk Small and round, in three coats: a little goat with the richest milk. Found in temperate meadows and plains.

Strays turn up in sheep country: plains, meadows, windswept hills. Wary, but meat wins them over, mutton best of all.

A colony lives in its hive and flies out to work flowers up to twelve blocks away, bringing nectar home. What the honey becomes depends on what they work: plant for it. Rain and winter keep them in. A hive with nothing i

Wild colonies nest in birch and oak, most of all in flower forests, and in savanna acacias. The kind is the country's, and a nest's colour tells you whose it is. An empty skep takes a nest's bees home with you.
The everyday bee of meadows and woods. Steady in every season, middling in temper. Wild in plains, forests and most temperate country. Plain golden nests.

The old dark bee of the north. Works through grey, cool weather and even a little in winter, but never makes much. Wild in the taiga and snowy country, in dark brown nests. Short-tempered: always smoke them.
Golden, gentle and the great honey-maker, but a hungry colony that eats its capped frames in winter. Wild in the savanna, nesting in acacias. Amber nests.
Grey and gentle bees of the mountains. The quickest of all to build up in spring. Wild in meadows, cherry groves and the hills. Grey-green nests.
A cross of Italian and Carniolan: gentle, hard-working, and easy to keep. Never found wild: see Breeding Buckfasts.
Woken out of amber, a bee lost for ages. Works steadily from early spring until the cold, and a little even in winter. Never found wild: only in amber, deep under old forests. Middling temper.

Seams of amber run in the rock under old forests. Once in a while a lump holds a bee, caught long ago. Hold it with an empty skep and it wakes: an ancient bee. Mine amber without silk touch, or you'll only get the seam.
How hard each works through the year, and its temper. Click a bee to turn to its page.
Hold an empty skep to a wild bee nest and use it: the bees come with it, of whatever kind lives there. A skep of bees can be carried and set down anywhere.
Straw, simple and old. When it's full, take honey with a bottle or comb with shears, like any hive. A skep has no frames: for named honeys you need a frame hive.
Put empty frames in (up to eight). As the hive fills, the bees draw them out and cap them with honey.
A sheet of paper in a frame of sticks. The bees build comb on it, fill it, and cap it with wax. No frames, no honey of its own: keep a few spare in.
Use a skep of bees on a frame hive to tip the colony in. The bees take the skep's kind with them.
Open a hive with an empty hand to look in: its bees, its frames, and what they're working. Lift capped frames out on its screen; smoke them first.
Smoke calms bees. Work with a campfire under the hive, a smoker in either hand, or Beekeeper's Calm. Without it, a colony may boil out and sting.

In spring a crowded colony sends half its bees off with the old queen. They hang in a buzzing cluster under a branch nearby. Hold an empty skep to it to catch it. Left alone, in a couple of days it moves into an empty hi
Keep Italian and Carniolan colonies within twenty-four blocks of each other. A swarm from either may come out Buckfast. Catch it and you have the gentlest, hardest-working bees of all.

Spring: colonies build up; fruit blossom and berry flowers. Summer: the main flow. Frames fill fast. Autumn: the flow slows; honeydew in the pines. Winter: clustered and still. Leave Italians something to eat.

Crop genetics: pollination, saving seed, and breeding better varieties.
Each runs from 0 to 15. An ordinary plant is about 7 or 8.
Every gene comes in two copies, one from each parent. The plant shows the average of the two. This plant looks ordinary, yet carries a fine copy it can pass on.

The bars show what its seedlings will show, on average. Gen counts how often the line has been saved. Breeds true: five dots and every seedling comes out alike. Fewer, and they scatter. Hover over a packet to read it.
Hold any seed and look at a crop: its genes show above your hotbar. It says too whether the plant has gone to seed. Walk your rows before harvest and note your best.
Each seed takes one copy of every gene from its mother, and one from the father whose pollen set it, by chance. Each square is one chance in four.
Wheat, beans, tomatoes and chillies pollinate themselves. A neighbour's pollen gets in only now and then. Their lines stay pure easily.
The wind crosses corn and beetroot: nearly every plant takes a neighbour's pollen. Insects cross these, about half the time; with bees near, nearly always.
Pollen travels this many blocks. Grow lines further apart to keep them pure.

Potatoes, garlic and sweet potatoes grow from the plant itself: the same plant again. Now and then a clone sports: one gene shifts on its own. A potato left to go to seed gives true seed you can cross.
Bees, or a hive within 16 blocks, carry pollen two blocks further and far more often. For pure seed, keep insect-crossed lines away from the hives.

Leave a ripe plant standing most of a day and it goes to seed: fluff drifts from it. Harvest it then for saved seed: its own genes and its pollen father's. More seed, less crop. Saved seed may not breed true.

Two different copies and the seedlings scatter. Two matched copies pass on every time. Save a line from itself a few years and it settles, and earns a name.
Cross two settled lines and every seedling gets one copy from each: an even first generation. A first cross grows strongly: hybrid vigour.
Save seed from that cross and the copies shuffle again: some take after one grandparent, some the other. Here are the surprises. Pick the best and start a new line.
Plants with mixed copies grow stronger. Crops that cross freely gain most from it. Inbred too long, those same crops grow weak. Selfers like wheat hardly mind inbreeding.

Some cave roofs are hung with glow-worm silk, beaded with soft blue light. Run about and they go dark; keep quiet and they come back. Shear silk for a lantern: bottle, silk, stick.
Pools of warm water deep down. A soak warms you right through. Drop in herbs or honey for an herbal bath:
Pale crystal glowing in deep hollows. Brush past and each rings its own note. Their shards make wind chimes.
Long dark rivers wind through the rock, deep enough for a boat, with a ledge to walk on. Blind cave fish bite there.
Old figures in ochre on the walls. Put paper to one to take a rubbing. Eight figures to find.
Seams under old forests. Now and then a lump holds a bee or a seed. Four amber make a glowing block.
Walk a pig on a lead in oak or birch woods: now and then it roots one up. Tamworths have the best noses.
Out in damp caves, and in the woods in rain. Cabbage tempts them; pick one up by hand. Cook one for escargot.
A log plugged with spawn fruits in the dark and damp: a cellar, or a cave by water. Lion's mane works too. Pick by hand.
Roots and apples kept three days in a crate somewhere cool and dark come out cellar-sweet. More filling than fresh.
A mead barrel deep in a cave ages half again as fast: the cold there is steady all year. The barrel says 'Cave cellar'.
In winter, in cold country, icicles grow on the roofs of caves near the surface. They melt in spring. Silk touch keeps one.
Blow it and the echo outlines the caves round you. Gold rings mean a way out. Good when you're lost.
Glow-worm lanterns light without smoke. A hot spring cures the winter chill. Keep gold nuggets for the new moon. Leave the knockers something nice.
